themes.label: Low-key spaces for casual socialization
themes.description: Participants value simple, local, and low-pressure spaces where they can naturally relax and be themselves with friends.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: nothing fancy, just a proper local.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: I think the main thing is it's just... low-key, you know? No one's trying too hard.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: somewhere you can just be yourself without it being a whole thing

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: almost harder to just... be somewhere casual, if that makes sense.

themes.label: Loss of local community spaces
themes.description: The closure of neighborhood spots makes spontaneous casual interactions harder and erodes local community connection.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: you end up just... staying in, I suppose. Or driving somewhere. Which defeats the purpose of having a local community space, doesn't it?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's not just about not having a pub nearby — it's that the whole casual social thing just... shrinks.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: You're not bumping into your mates by accident like you might have done if there was something local.

themes.label: Spontaneous hangouts replaced by planned events
themes.description: As local social hubs disappear, friendships shift from spontaneous, frequent gatherings to scheduled high-pressure events supplemented by superficial messaging.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: hanging out face-to-face becomes this thing that has to be scheduled weeks in advance.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: You go from seeing each other pretty regularly just because you're around, to it being like... you've got to book a date three weeks out and make it count.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: we message loads now, but it's not the same.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: I've definitely noticed friendships feel a bit thinner when it's just that.

themes.label: Commercialization and curation of social venues
themes.description: Venues have become increasingly themed, highly curated, or expensive, which creates social pressure and detracts from the ease of simply hanging out.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: a lot of them are either quite... I dunno, themed up or whatever, or they've got this vibe where you feel like you should be spending more money or dressed a certain way.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: everything's still there, right, but it's either a Wetherspoons or some fancy cocktail place, or it's in Broad Street where it costs you thirty quid before you've even sat down. Or it's got this whole vibe attached to it — you know what I mean? It's not just a place you go, it's a thing.

themes.label: Anxiety and paralysis of digital food choices
themes.description: Participants discuss how the overwhelming abundance of choices on delivery apps, combined with the isolated nature of screen-based ordering, leads to overthinking, decision paralysis, and constant self-doubt.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: But when there's that much choice it's almost paralyzing, you know? Like, any decision you make feels like you're missing out on something better.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's not just about choice — it's that the choice is happening in isolation, on a screen, where you're constantly aware you could pick something else.

themes.label: Loss of local independent food establishments
themes.description: Participants highlight how unique local food spots are disappearing and being replaced by corporate chains, resulting in a narrower range of actual food variety despite the illusion of choice offered by apps.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: honestly the issue for me isn't having too many options — it's more that a lot of the decent independent places have either shut or they're changing into chains.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: your actual choice has got narrower, but the apps are trying to make out there's more, and it's just... the same stuff repeated.

themes.label: Decline of community connection in dining
themes.description: The transition to app-based ordering is described as creating a highly transactional and cold experience that strips away the social connections and sense of community once fostered by visiting local food spots.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: It's becoming more... transactional. You're ordering through an app from your house, it arrives, you eat it alone probably, and there's no actual connection to anywhere or anyone.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: Everything's efficient now, and I get why that's meant to be better, but it's also kind of cold. You're not part of anywhere. You're just a customer moving through the system.

themes.label: Complicity in losing local food spaces
themes.description: Participants grapple with the guilt of using convenient delivery apps while lamenting the decline of physical, community-oriented food spaces.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's weird because you feel powerless — like, what am I gonna do, not use Deliveroo? — but you're also kind of complicit in killing off the thing you're saying you miss.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: The complicity thing Ibrahim mentioned — that's real. But it's only relevant while there's still something to be complicit in losing, if that makes sense.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: But you're still choosing that easier thing knowing what the alternative is costing. That's different to inheriting a situation that's already gone, I think.

themes.label: Gendered social pressure and public eating
themes.description: Men describe feeling self-conscious eating alone or choosing non-traditional foods in public spaces, often turning to delivery apps to escape social judgment.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Is it weird if I'm a bloke just sat eating by myself? And I think that's maybe where the app thing actually works, in a weird way.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: You're kind of aware you're a bloke sat alone, and you're thinking... I dunno, are people thinking I'm a weirdo?

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: Like, I can order a curry or a kebab or chips and no one's gonna clock it as weird. That's just normal bloke food, right? But if I'm getting like... I dunno, a salad, or something that looks fancy or a bit fussy, there's this wee voice in your head going, is this a bit much?

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: Because if you're in a pub full of blokes and you're visibly ordering something they think is soft or fussy, you're not just getting judged quietly. You're getting proper taken the piss out of.

themes.label: Veganism as a loaded moral statement
themes.description: Choosing vegetarian or vegan food is perceived as a visible statement of identity and values that invites social interrogation, unlike ordering simpler light options.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: Like, if I ordered vegan food, that's not just about the food. That's got all this other stuff attached to it — like, you're making a statement, right? You're being preachy, or you're one of those people, or you're trying too hard.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: The vegan thing especially — it's not just about being seen eating something. It's about what people assume you're saying about yourself by eating it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Because yeah, there's self-consciousness about being a bloke eating alone or eating something that looks fussy. But the vegan thing — that forces a conversation. It makes you legible as someone with a particular set of beliefs or commitments, and then people either want to argue with you about it or they want to know your whole reasoning.

themes.label: Apps as a short-term trap
themes.description: Food ordering apps provide immediate relief from social anxieties but ultimately erode public spaces and foster long-term dependency.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It takes away the anxiety, the performance, the worry about what people are gonna think. And that's a genuine thing it's solving. But it solves it by removing you from the picture entirely, which is part of what's killing off the actual spaces where you wouldn't need to solve it in the first place.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: the app's a short-term fix that makes the long-term thing worse.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: The issue is that people are choosing the app instead, choosing to stay home, so the places where that could be normal are losing the people who would make it normal.

themes.label: Real social costs of visibility
themes.description: Making unconventional dietary choices in close-knit communities carries genuine social consequences, making individual defiance too costly.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: The Grapes or whatever might still be open, but it's still a bloke's pub. That's the culture of it. That's not changing because a few people decide to order plant-based. And the other thing is — it's not just about the pub itself, right? It's about your actual community.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: The reflex isn't getting stronger because I'm not testing it. It's staying strong because testing it would actually cost me something.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's that principle only works if you can actually afford the cost of it, and you can't.

themes.label: Internalized reflexes and comfortable invisibility
themes.description: Social pressure becomes an automatic reflex that blocks certain choices, and food apps allow people to retreat into comfortable invisibility rather than confront this pressure.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I'll be scrolling through and I'll see something, and there'll be this just quick thing in my head — nah, not that — without me really having to consciously decide. It's become reflex.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: I'm not testing anything. I'm just... staying invisible. And every time I do it, the invisibility gets more comfortable

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: I'll be scrolling through the app and there'll be something and I just automatically go nah, not that, and I won't even properly think about why

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: I just stay home, order what I want alone, and never have to test whether the pressure's as real as I think it is.

themes.label: Invisible performance of public visibility
themes.description: Even in neutral or non-judgmental public spaces, the awareness of being visible and supporting a space creates a subtle, self-conscious form of social performance.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: even being in that space, there's still this awareness that I'm part of making it happen, right? Like, I'm not just existing in that space, I'm also aware that my choice to be there, to order something plant-based or whatever, is part of what keeps that space existing.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: even in the space where it's meant to be normal, if you're aware that you're part of making it work, there's still this layer of... performance. Just invisible.

themes.label: Waiting for others to normalize change
themes.description: Participants confess that they are waiting for someone else to take the social risk and absorb the discomfort of ordering plant-based food first before they will do so themselves.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It works because someone else does it first and then it just becomes normal.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I'm waiting for someone else to make it safe first.

themes.label: Intellectual awareness versus actual behavior change
themes.description: Speakers struggle with a frustrating disconnect between intellectually understanding their choices and actually taking action to change their behavior.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: knowing it feels a bit hollow. It doesn't actually move anything.

valid_quotes.quote: I don't know if I'm gonna do anything different either. But yeah, saying it out loud like this — it's harder to pretend it's just how things are.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: The difference between recognizing a trap and being stuck in it — I get that now. I recognize it. But I'm not actually getting out of it.

themes.label: Avoiding visibility and identity performance
themes.description: Participants express a desire to avoid having their dietary choices perceived as a statement or performance of a specific social identity.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Because if I commit to ordering plant-based, that means something about me, right? Even if it's not a huge thing. And I'm not sure I want to be that visible.

themes.label: The pub as an effortless social default
themes.description: Gathering at the pub serves as the default option for friends because it is convenient, requires no advance planning, and allows people to drop in and leave flexibly.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Yeah, the pub's definitely the default for us too.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: The pub you can just rock up, have a couple, leave when you want.

themes.label: Valuing active and intentional interactions
themes.description: Engaging in structured or alternative activities, such as cooking at home together, encourages deeper conversations and creates more memorable experiences than passive pub routines.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: But I've noticed people are keener now on actually doing stuff rather than just... sitting in the same bar every time.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: With the cooking thing, even if it's a hassle to organize, there's actually something happening. You're talking properly, making food, eating together. Versus the pub where you're just... drinking and watching whoever's match is on.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Those stick with you more than just another pint night, don't they? I think it's just... the pub is so easy to default to that you don't really question it. But you're saying something real there about actually being present.

themes.label: Defaulting to familiar routines
themes.description: Participants describe a tendency to stick to familiar, habitual choices for food and social venues rather than actively making decisions or exploring new options.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Even when I'm thinking I should try something different, I don't really. It's just easier to stick with what works.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Whether it's because there's literally nothing else or because trying something new requires more effort than just getting what you know — the end result's pretty similar. You're not choosing, you're just doing what's easiest.

themes.label: Geographic vs. situational constraints on choice
themes.description: The discussion compares how physical isolation in rural settings and cognitive fatigue or effort in urban settings both act as barriers to trying new things.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's just... logistics are a bit different when you're not in a city with loads of options, you know?

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Because yeah, there's only one shop out here, but it's not like I'm sat at home thinking "I could drive twenty minutes to the next town if I really wanted to." That's just not realistic for a weeknight when you're knackered after work.

themes.label: Norm of masculine nonchalance toward food
themes.description: Men face a social expectation to appear casual or indifferent about their food choices rather than appearing overly invested, fussy, or passionate about cooking and ingredients.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's more of a bloke thing to just eat what's put in front of you, not make a fuss about it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's not that you genuinely don't care about food out here. It's that you can't be seen to care too much, because that looks like you're being a bit precious about it.

themes.label: Self-policing to maintain social reputation
themes.description: To avoid social judgment, mockery, or gossip within close-knit networks, men actively self-censor their food choices and internalize societal expectations.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: The social cost of being seen to care too much feels bigger than just... sticking with what you know. It's easier to default than to risk being labeled as that guy.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: You can't just move to a different part of town or go to a different social circle where people don't know that side of you. Everyone knows everyone, and they've got long memories.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: You're policing yourself so hard you don't even see the bars.

themes.label: Gendered categorization of food types
themes.description: Certain foods, such as salads or colorful and delicate dishes, are perceived as feminine or 'soft,' leading men to default to more substantial options like meat and burgers.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: Same with like, anything that's too colorful or has flowers on it or whatever — like, I've been to places where they've got these nice plates with edible flowers and that, and it just feels weird to order it as a bloke. You'd look a bit soft doing that.

themes.label: Plant-based eating and male identity
themes.description: Choosing plant-based foods is often perceived as unmasculine or "soft" compared to standard, culturally approved male behaviors.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: like, I'll be looking at a menu and there's something that looks decent but it's got salad on the side or it's a bit... I dunno, refined or whatever, and there's this immediate thought of like, nah, that's not really a bloke order, is it?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: With the vegan thing, there's still that undertone of like... it's not normal, it's a bit soft or whatever. Whereas supporting a football team is just... normal.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Like you're thinking about animals or ethics or where your food's coming from, and that just reads as a bit soft when you're a bloke.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: But caring about whether your food's vegan? That reads as like, you're worried about hurting something, or you're being precious about it, or you care too much about stuff that doesn't really matter in a manly way.

themes.label: Permanent dietary identity in peer groups
themes.description: Committing to a plant-based diet creates a persistent social identity within groups, making the choice feel heavy and difficult to reverse.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But if you're the bloke who's gone vegan or vegetarian or whatever, that's a thing about you now. That's your identity in the group.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: But if you go vegetarian or vegan, it's not just about the food anymore. It becomes who you are. It becomes something people know about you, something they bring up.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Once it's a thing about you, you're kind of committed to it in a way you wouldn't be otherwise. Because if you suddenly go back to eating meat, that's another thing — that's you changing your mind, that's you failing at it or whatever people think.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It becomes a permanent part of how you're seen in the group. And that's not the same as people constantly taking the piss about it. It's just that it's always there, you know?

themes.label: Social bubbles and dietary acceptance
themes.description: The level of acceptance or judgment for plant-based eating is heavily dependent on specific peer groups, education, and social class.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3

And in those spaces, caring about where your food comes from or going vegan — it's kind of expected.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I'm saying in the specific circles I move in, it is. And I think that's probably because of who those people are, not because Edinburgh's just more progressive or whatever.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It might be more normalized in certain groups, certain parts of the city maybe, but that doesn't mean it's just... normal now across the board.

themes.label: Normalizing plant-based food presentation
themes.description: Plant-based food should be presented like normal, everyday food to remove the alternative lifestyle signal that prevents people from ordering it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: a lot of it feels like it's made to be vegan first and to be good second, you know? Like the priority's all wrong.

themes.label: Challenging perceived social barriers
themes.description: The social awkwardness and judgment surrounding plant-based eating are often overestimated and tend to dissolve once individuals actually try the food.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Maybe people just need to... try it more and realize it's not as big a deal as they thought.

themes.label: Preferring 'someone's yard' for socializing

valid_quotes.quote: The yard's just... there. You can just roll round whenever and it's free. Plus you can stay as long as you want without anyone kicking you out or whatever.

valid_quotes.quote: At the yard you can just... chill properly. Play some games, have a laugh, not have to think about anything.

themes.label: Comfort versus stagnation in social routines
themes.description: While meeting in private spaces is highly comfortable, it can lead to stagnation, repetitive social patterns, and a lack of new experiences.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: The yard's definitely more relaxed, you don't have to worry about anything. But like... I dunno, sometimes I think you get a bit stuck in it, you know? Like, me and my mates, we've been doing the same thing for ages now — same people, same yard, same games.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

themes.label: Active choice versus routine socialization
themes.description: Participants debate whether transitioning away from hanging out at a friend's house as they get older is a conscious choice for new experiences or a reaction to a stale routine.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But now, I dunno, you just get sick of it after a bit, don't you? Same conversations, same people saying the same jokes. It starts to feel a bit... stale.

valid_quotes.quote: Like, there's a difference between "I got bored so I had to leave" and "I want to do this thing," you know? They're not the same headspace.

themes.label: Geographical influences on social planning
themes.description: Living in rural areas imposes constraints that require deliberate planning and intentionality, whereas urban environments offer spontaneous choices that can be easily taken for granted.

valid_quotes.quote: you're not just choosing to cook at home because you fancy it, you're doing it because that's what's actually there, you know? That's a proper constraint, not just a preference.

valid_quotes.quote: You're rationalizing it as a choice when really you're just... going along with what feels safest.

valid_quotes.quote: You lose the spontaneity but you maybe gain something else, like actually being intentional about your choices instead of just defaulting to whatever's easiest.

themes.label: Accepting banter as a social cost
themes.description: Participants discuss how choosing non-conforming food options involves accepting lighthearted teasing from friends as a natural social cost, rather than feeling forced to conform or pretending not to care.

themes.label: Structural barriers to plant-based eating

themes.label: Invisibility of Unfamiliar Lifestyles

themes.label: Urban Versus Rural Environmental Influences

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

themes.label: The comfort of a default venue

themes.label: Trust, belonging, and social ease

themes.label: Seeking spaces to avoid social performance

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Sometimes you just want to not be visible, kind of. Not performing. That's a different reason to keep going back to the same place, isn't it?

themes.label: Practicality and convenience in food choices

themes.label: Habits versus lack of geographic choice

themes.label: Influence of Social Familiarity and Context
themes.description: The self-consciousness regarding food choices decreases in relaxed settings or around familiar peers, but recurs when dining with unfamiliar people.

themes.label: Rational Knowledge Versus Persistent Social Awareness
themes.description: Although participants logically recognize that others do not care what they eat, the emotional or psychological awareness of being observed persists and influences behavior.

themes.label: Local Visibility and Lack of Anonymity

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

themes.label: Single choices versus social identity

valid_quotes.speaker: P3

themes.label: Relevance of barriers without desire
themes.description: Perceived lifestyle barriers are not experienced as true constraints when a person has no genuine motivation or interest in changing their behavior.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

themes.label: Constant social visibility of dietary choices

valid_quotes.speaker: P3

themes.label: Using practical excuses to mask social conformity

themes.label: Decoupling plant-based food from identity

themes.label: Routine versus flexible planning

valid_quotes.speaker: P5

themes.label: Relational tension in families

themes.label: Responsibility beyond the individual

themes.label: Collective transition versus isolation

themes.label: Context-dependent daily eating decisions

themes.description: Regardless of whether they live in areas with abundant options or restricted choices, people tend to default to the same social routines and venues, making the presence of choice mostly theoretical.

valid_quotes.quote: I've just settled into the routine with my mates at the same place, and I've not really thought about whether there are actual alternatives or if I've just stopped looking because it's easier not to. And you're right — when you put it like that, the difference between having a choice available and choosing not to bother versus just not having it at all gets a bit blurry for me.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: I go to the same pub with the same people, end up ordering the same kind of thing. And I never really question it because the options are there, so I assume I'm choosing. But I'm probably not choosing at all — I'm just doing the default thing like everyone else.

themes.label: Logistical hurdles of plant-based eating
themes.description: Transitioning to a plant-based diet requires significant effort, cooking knowledge, and time to seek out options, adding an unwelcome mental burden to daily food decisions.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: I'd need to actually know what to eat. Like, I don't cook much. Most of my eating is just grabbing something quick or ordering takeaway or going to the pub. I haven't got the knowledge or the routine around it to suddenly do plant-based.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Going plant-based would mean actually thinking about it every time I eat, and I'm not sure I've got the headspace for that.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Yeah, and I think what Bilal's saying about the logistics is real — you'd have to actually learn stuff, find places, all that.

themes.label: Social friction of being different
themes.description: Transitioning to plant-based eating involves stepping out of the comfortable default, which subjects an individual to social scrutiny and forces them to make an active, visible choice every time they eat.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Like, the pub thing on its own — that's already hard because everyone's ordering burgers and that. If I went plant-based, that's a whole different dynamic, isn't it. You're the one person ordering something different, and yeah, you'd definitely get comments.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But if you went plant-based, suddenly every single time you're eating, you're making a statement about it. You're the one ordering something different. You're the one choosing. And I think that's harder than just... not having to own it, you know?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Right now the routine protects you from that. You're just following what everyone else does. You're not picking a position on it, you're just... going along.

themes.label: Choosing within constraints versus questioning constraints
themes.description: Participants debate whether their food habits represent passive conformity or active preferences, drawing a distinction between picking from existing options and fundamentally questioning their diet.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: You're still choosing — you're just choosing the path of least resistance sometimes. That's not the same as not choosing at all.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: You're making choices within a set of options that's already there. That's not the same as actually deciding, like, should I eat plant-based? Should I change what I'm eating fundamentally?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's not that you've got no agency. It's just that you're using that agency to move around within the constraints, not to question the constraints themselves.

themes.label: Ongoing friction and practical costs
themes.description: Transitioning to plant-based eating is perceived as a continuous, high-effort commitment with real daily social and practical costs.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But going plant-based when everyone around you isn't? That's not just a choice you make once. That's you having to actively manage it every time you eat, every time you're out with people.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's more that once you actually understand what it would cost — the effort, the social stuff — you're not sure you want to do it.

themes.label: Plant-based food as a compromise
themes.description: Plant-based options are often viewed as unsatisfying substitutes and a culinary compromise rather than proper food that men actually want.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: plant-based stuff, for a lot of blokes like us, just doesn't feel like proper food, you know?

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: going plant-based isn't about choosing something better. It's about choosing something that's supposed to be better for you, but tastes like less.

themes.label: Rationalizing inaction through assumed barriers
themes.description: Participants self-reflectively realize that the barriers they list are unverified assumptions used to justify a simple lack of effort to change.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: I've never really tried it properly, have I? Like, I'm sitting here saying it tastes like a compromise, that it doesn't feel like real food. But I haven't actually... I haven't actually eaten much plant-based stuff.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I've been listing barriers like they're facts, but they're more like... things I think would be barriers because I haven't bothered to find out.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: I think I might be listing them because I've already decided I'm not going to bother, and I need it to sound like a rational choice rather than just... not bothering.

themes.label: Local Embeddedness as Practical Security
themes.description: Participants explain how long-term familiarity, local networks, and recognized routines provide essential, practical support and security, especially as parents age.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: If something happens to him, if he falls or has a bad day, there are people on the street who know them. The GP's local. The pharmacy. It's all sort of woven in.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: knowing where you belong, where people know you.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: That he's settled where he is, people know him. That matters.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: There's my mum's friends who check in, and they're not checking in because they feel like they should — they actually know what he's dealing with because they live it. They see him shuffle to the shop and know something's changed. That's not just comfort. That takes years to build.

themes.label: The Pub as an Informal Social Hub
themes.description: The local pub is highlighted as the primary place for male friends to gather because it offers a relaxed, familiar environment that requires very little active planning.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: You don't have to plan much, just... you know where people will be.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: the pub, same as Nick really.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: Don't have to text anyone or plan it out — you just know roughly when people will be there, and if they're not today they'll probably be there next week.

themes.label: Distinguishing Security From Comfortable Habit
themes.description: A tension is raised over whether remaining in a familiar area is a source of true security or simply a comfortable habit that can leave people feeling trapped or locked in.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: But you're also kind of locked in, aren't you? Like, you've all said you've been here ages, people are drifting away, lives are getting more fixed around the same few places.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: knowing your neighbours is one thing, but a lot of that is just habit. It's comfortable. And comfort's fine, but I'm not convinced it's the same as security, if that makes sense.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Look, comfort and habit — yeah, fair enough, that's part of it. I'm not going to pretend I haven't just settled here because it's easy. But it's not the same thing as security, and I don't think that's just me rationalizing.

themes.label: Familiarity versus active support
themes.description: Participants argue that being socially embedded in a neighborhood provides comfort and a foundation, but does not guarantee active assistance during a crisis.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: don't mistake knowing people for them actually being there when it matters.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: The embedded thing helped, but it didn't replace actual... people doing things, you know?

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: Knowing people and them actually being there when something matters are two different things.

themes.label: Loneliness within familiar environments
themes.description: The speakers observe that having established routines and being well-known in a community does not prevent deep, personal loneliness.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: You can be embedded somewhere and still be quite alone, you know?

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: The routine just meant he was lonely in a familiar place.

themes.label: Shared eating as social connection
themes.description: Participants contrast the loneliness of grabbing quick food alone with the meaningful connection of sharing a meal with others.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: if you're eating alone most nights, if you're just grabbing whatever's easiest, that's — I don't know, that's a kind of loneliness in itself, isn't it?

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: When I'm with my dad we might just have beans on toast or whatever, but it feels different because it's not just fuel.

themes.label: Shared meals do not cure persistent loneliness
themes.description: Occasional shared meals, while positive, do not solve underlying loneliness and can make returning to isolation feel more difficult.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But it doesn't fix the loneliness the rest of the time, you know? It can actually make it worse sometimes, because you get that hit of — someone cares, someone's here — and then you go back to eating alone and it stings a bit more.

themes.label: Lack of social expectation for men to cook
themes.description: Men experience less social pressure or expectation to know how to cook, which can lead to a state of casual uselessness where they rely on convenience foods.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: No one's judging you for not knowing how to cook or not bothering. Whereas if my wife just lived on takeaways and freezer stuff, there'd be this... I don't know, this sense she should be doing better, managing it properly.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: And that sounds like a good thing, doesn't it — freedom, not being nagged about it. But I think what that actually does is — it lets you off the hook in a way that isn't really good for you.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: And I've just — I've never bothered to get better at it because there's no pressure, like you said. It's just easier to not learn.

themes.label: Cooking as connection and care
themes.description: Cooking is viewed as an essential life skill that facilitates self-care, caring for others, and inviting social connections rather than just consuming food as fuel.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Because if you don't cook, you don't invite people over for meals. You don't learn how to do something for someone else. You're just feeding yourself fuel. And that's a kind of — I don't know, a kind of disconnection, isn't it?

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: It does feed into the loneliness, the isolation. You're not learning how to invite people over, or sit down and actually make something.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's about — knowing how to look after yourself. Knowing how to do something that takes time, that you do for someone else.

themes.label: Intergenerational transmission of not cooking
themes.description: Men observe their fathers not cooking and pass this pattern of non-cooking and self-neglect down to their own sons.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: He's fourteen. And he watches me not cook. He watches me not knowing how to do it. And he's already the same way. He can't be bothered, he doesn't think he needs to learn it, because Dad doesn't do it either, so why would he?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: I didn't have kids, but I think about my dad sometimes. And he was the same — didn't cook, didn't think he needed to. And I grew up watching that.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Because he's watching you, and he's going to do the same thing, and then his kids are going to do it. And it just keeps going.

themes.label: Cooking to connect and care
themes.description: Participants view learning to cook as a meaningful way to connect with and care for their children and aging parents, passing down essential life skills.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's about — showing him that you can do something for yourself. That you can sit down and make something that takes time, that means something.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Paul's named something real there, about it passing down, about not knowing how to look after someone else through food. That's not small. I've got kids too, and I'm thinking the same thing now.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I don't want to get to sixty and realize I never learned how to do something that basic for someone I care about. So the plant-based thing — I don't know. But the cooking thing. Yeah. That needs to happen.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: I don't want to get to where my dad is — where I'm visiting him and I can't actually do anything with food that means something. That's not about the diet, that's about — I don't know, being able to actually look after someone properly.

themes.label: Prioritizing relational cooking over dietary changes
themes.description: Speakers explicitly resist the moderator's shift to hypothetical questions about plant-based eating, emphasizing that relational cooking is more urgent and fundamental.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: So I don't know if I want to jump to the plant-based question right now, because I'm actually thinking I need to — not in a dramatic way, but I need to learn how to actually cook something. Not hypothetically. Actually do it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: Look, I'm going to be honest — I'm not really thinking about plant-based right now, because what's just been said about the cooking, about Daniel and his son, that's what I'm sitting with.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: The plant-based thing feels like the wrong thing to be focused on right now, because what's actually sitting with me is what you're all saying about the cooking.

themes.label: The difficulty of sustaining habit change
themes.description: Participants discuss the tension between emotional intentions and the practical, exhausting reality of breaking long-standing habits.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: But what actually happens is — life gets in the way. Work gets mad. You're tired. You forget why it mattered so much. Or you try once or twice and it's awkward, or your dad's busy, or you just — you slip back into what's easy because it's easier.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I don't do it every week. I forget sometimes, work's mad, all of that. But I've done it enough now that it's a thing. It's something that happens. And it does matter.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: I'm not saying don't try. I'm saying — I understand why it felt important in this moment. But I also know what it's like when the person you're trying to do it for is already slipping. And that's a different kind of hard than just — you're busy, you forget, you try again next week.

themes.label: Social proof and personal cooking
themes.description: Participants believe dietary changes happen when trusted individuals cook and share good food, rather than through industry marketing.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: So what would actually move the needle isn't packaging or marketing or whatever. It's — someone you actually know, someone normal, making something that tastes good and having people over to eat it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: That's not marketing. That's not some campaign trying to convince blokes that plant-based is masculine or whatever nonsense. That's just — someone you know, someone normal, doing something decent and it working.

themes.label: Inertia of comfortable social routines
themes.description: Established social routines like meeting at the pub present a strong path of least resistance, making the effort to cook and host friends difficult to initiate.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: the routine is so easy that you don't bother disrupting it. You finish work, you're tired, you meet the lads at the pub like you always do. That's the path of least resistance.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: part of it is what Nick said — the routine's easier. You just meet at the pub, that's what happens.

themes.label: Social vulnerability of peer cooking
themes.description: Cooking for male friends introduces a unique sense of vulnerability, exposure, and fear of judgment that is absent in neutral social settings or family dynamics.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But your house, you cooking something, expecting them to show up and eat it — that's different. That's you doing something for them, and there's a vulnerability in that, I think.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: But because there's something about doing it with mates that feels a bit exposed. Like you're admitting you want to do something different, something that matters a bit, and that opens you up to — I don't know, judgment? Being thought of as soft?

themes.label: Imperfect action in family caregiving
themes.description: When caring for family, making a flawed or awkward attempt to cook is valued over the risk of failure or not trying at all.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: I'd rather try and mess it up half the time than not try at all and know for certain I missed it. I think that's what's different. Not that it's easy. Just that not doing it now feels worse than trying and getting it wrong sometimes.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4
valid_quotes.quote: With my old man, if the food's not great, it doesn't matter. He's just — he's glad I'm there, glad we're doing it. It's not about whether I'm a brilliant cook. It's about the fact that I'm trying. That I showed up and made an effort.

themes.label: Valuing ordinary and unpretentious settings
themes.description: Participants express a preference for everyday, unfancy environments like homes, gardens, and local football matches over more elaborate or performative settings.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But honestly, we probably spend more time just round someone's house or at the football.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's the ordinary stuff, like Andrew said. Not Instagram-worthy, but it's where you actually are.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Nobody's dressing it up to be anything other than what it is, and that's fine. That's just... life, really.

themes.label: Safe spaces for vulnerable conversations
themes.description: Informal and relaxed gatherings, such as sitting in a garden, create comfortable opportunities for men to discuss personal struggles and check in on each other without pressure.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But that's where the real conversation happens, you know? Where you actually find out how your mate's getting on with something, or you're just comfortable enough to be a bit vulnerable without making a big deal of it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: One of them's going through a rough patch with his missus at the moment, and you talk about it properly, but it's not some deep therapy session either, you know? You just... you're there. You're listening.

themes.label: Escaping roles and performing expectations
themes.description: Spending time with long-term male friends allows men to shed the professional and domestic responsibilities they feel pressured to perform in other parts of their lives.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's about that permission to just be normal with someone. Not performing, not having to be the bloke at work or the dad at home.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: With work, you've got to be competent, professional, whatever. At home with the family there's all the stuff that needs managing — I've got a grown-up kid and my wife's got her own things going on, and you're just... you're performing that role.

themes.label: Friendship as a mental health necessity
themes.description: Spending casual, unstructured time with long-term friends is described as crucial for maintaining sanity, keeping going, and avoiding emotional tightness.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's not exciting but it's... it's important. That's the bit that keeps you sane, I reckon.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: And yeah, that's what keeps you going, I think. Without that, you'd just be grinding through, wouldn't you?

valid_quotes.speaker: P1

valid_quotes.speaker: P3

themes.label: Desire for everyday decision-making autonomy
themes.description: Participants express a desire for small moments of independent choice in their routine, free from the constant need to consult, negotiate, or coordinate with others.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: But there's times when I think, I'd like to just... decide. Not even to eat something different necessarily, just to have made the decision, you know? It's a small thing, but it matters.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: It's just that small thing of having made a choice and nobody's questioning it or you're not fitting it around what someone else has already planned.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: But there's definitely times I think, I'd just like to have picked something and that be the end of it. No negotiation.

themes.label: The value of shared family meals
themes.description: Sitting down at the table together is valued as a meaningful, unhurried space for genuine connection and conversation.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: Because when you're actually sat down with people, even if it's just the family and you're having an ordinary Tuesday night dinner, you can actually talk.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: And that feels like a thing, you know? It matters. It's not about the food being special, it's just... you're doing it together without any rush.

themes.label: Self-policing masculine food expectations

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: I wouldn't order a salad at a restaurant with my wife there without feeling a bit self-conscious about it. Or like, I wouldn't eat a yoghurt as a lunch without thinking it looked a bit... I don't know. Soft?

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: You've got this picture in your head of what you're supposed to be eating as a bloke, and even if nobody's actually saying it, you're kind of policing yourself around it.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: Like, what does this say about me? Which is daft because it's a salad, it's just food. But there's this running commentary going on in your head, and it's not your wife saying it, like you said — it's you.

themes.label: Gradual erosion of personal agency
themes.description: Men discuss how repeatedly conceding minor everyday decisions to keep the peace can gradually accumulate, leading to a loss of personal agency and self-erasure in long-term relationships.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But there's a difference between compromise and just... checking out of your own decisions, isn't there?

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: It's like a habit of shrinking yourself a bit in certain spaces. With your wife, with family, you're managing how you come across.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: Am I checking in because I'm trying not to be selfish, or because I've just given up having opinions about anything? Because those feel like different things to me.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: But there's a point where you stop pushing back on anything because you don't want it to become a thing, and then you've basically decided that keeping the peace is more important than having your own say.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: You check in here, you don't mention what you'd actually like there, you eat the salad and don't say anything because it's easier — and after a while, you're not even sure what you'd want if nobody was watching. That's the trap in it.

themes.label: Conflating consideration with personal disappearance
themes.description: Participants discuss how trying to be easygoing and considerate has led them to stop expressing preferences, effectively disappearing from decision-making in their own lives.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's not about the food. It's that I don't know where being considerate stops and just... disappearing starts. And I'm not sure I've noticed where that line is in my own house.

valid_quotes.speaker: P2
valid_quotes.quote: It's me having to stop being invisible in my own decisions.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: But listening to Andrew say that — about stopping being invisible — I'm starting to see that's not actually easier. It just feels that way in the moment. Because you're not dealing with anything becoming a thing. But the cost is that you're not actually in your own life.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: When did I stop deciding things? When did I decide that keeping things smooth was more important than actually mattering in my own life?

themes.label: Self-censorship to avoid relational friction
themes.description: Participants admit to pre-emptively suppressing their own thoughts and managing partners' reactions to avoid negotiation or conflict, sometimes internalizing these boundaries completely.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: I'm managing her reaction before I've even decided what I think. And that's... that's not considerate, is it? That's just me not having a voice.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: But the truth is I'd like to go in the summer. It matters to me. But I haven't said that because it's another thing to negotiate, and it's easier not to.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: It's that I've internalized the boundary so much that I'm not even letting myself have the opinion in the first place.

themes.label: Negotiation and compromise versus self-effacement
themes.description: A counter-perspective is introduced, distinguishing between healthy marital compromise where views are negotiated and a dysfunctional dynamic where speaking up is not permitted.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: You can be in a partnership where you actually negotiate things — where you have preferences, you say them, and sometimes they win and sometimes they don't — without it being this big statement about whether you matter or not. That's just... being married. That's compromise.

valid_quotes.speaker: P5
valid_quotes.quote: The question is — can you actually say what you think without it blowing up? Can you have a different opinion without your wife treating it like a betrayal? themes.label: Conflating consideration with personal absence
themes.description: Participants realize that what they have been calling 'being considerate' has actually been an absence of their own opinions and presence.

valid_quotes.speaker: P1
valid_quotes.quote: That's not about being considerate. That's about having lost the ability to know what you actually want.

valid_quotes.speaker: P3
valid_quotes.quote: I've stopped letting myself know what I want because it's easier not to, and now I genuinely can't tell the difference between being considerate and just being absent.

valid_quotes.speaker: P4

themes.label: Managing conversations with safe answers

valid_quotes.speaker: P2

themes.label: Action versus reflection in reclaiming agency
themes.description: Participants debate whether reclaiming their agency requires speaking first and figuring things out through action, or reflecting first to ensure their voice is authentic and not just reactive.
